passages.title: Global Design Competition
content:
John needs help preparing for his [ _____ ].
The professor advises him to build a [ _____ ] of the design.
John’s main difficulty is obtaining good-quality [ _____ ].
The professor recommends applying for a [ _____ ].
The professor will check the [ _____ ] information in John’s written report.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a university student discussing an entry for a global design competition with the professor. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
[00:54] JOHN: Hello, professor. I'm John Wishart. I'm preparing my entry for the global design competition, and my tutor suggested that you might help.
[01:03] PROFESSOR: Yes, I received your drawings. Come in and explain the project. What does the competition involve?
[01:11] JOHN: It's an international contest. Entrance must propose a new design for an ordinary domestic kitchen appliance.
[01:19] PROFESSOR: Are there any special requirements, such as reducing energy use?
[01:24] JOHN: Energy efficiency was last year's theme. This time we must take existing technology and find a genuinely new application for it.
[01:35] PROFESSOR: That sounds demanding. Which appliance did you select?
[01:39] JOHN: A dishwasher. They're common in Australian homes, but most models look dull and nearly identical. I think customers would pay slightly more for one with greater visual appeal.
[01:52] PROFESSOR: You call the design rock pool. Why?
[01:56] JOHN: Its appearance resembles a rock pool at the beach. A glass top lets you look inside.
[02:02] PROFESSOR: There's also a stone at the bottom. Is it decorative?
[02:07] JOHN: It serves a purpose. You rotate the stone instead of pressing a switch to start the machine.
[02:13] PROFESSOR: So that is an unusual starting control. What is the main innovation?
[02:18] JOHN: The dishwasher uses carbon dioxide.
[02:22] PROFESSOR: Instead of water and detergent, how?
[02:26] JOHN: The carbon dioxide is pressurised until it becomes liquid. It then enters the dishwasher and cleans the dishes.
[02:34] PROFESSOR: That would remove the need for powerful detergents. What happens after cleaning?

[02:41] JOHN: The liquid carbon dioxide and waste flow into a holding chamber while the dishes dry. Depressurising the liquid converts it back into a gas. Oil and grease are separated and sent into the waste system.
[02:55] PROFESSOR: And what happens to the carbon dioxide at the end? I hope it isn't discarded.
[03:01] JOHN: No. It returns to the cylinder, ready to be used repeatedly.
[03:06] PROFESSOR: An excellent idea. Will the machine ever be manufactured?
[03:11] JOHN: Probably not, but I don't mind.
[03:12] PROFESSOR: The project should still produce useful results.
[03:20] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
[04:06] PROFESSOR: You appear to have considered the design thoroughly. What help do you need from me?
[04:11] JOHN: The entry has reached the final stage. In a few months, I must give a presentation, and I'd like help preparing it.
[04:20] PROFESSOR: That should be manageable. What have you completed so far?
[04:24] JOHN: I have detailed drawings explaining the operation, as well as a 500-word paper.
[04:30] PROFESSOR: To have a strong chance of winning, you should also build a model.
[04:35] JOHN: I agree, but I've run into difficulties.
[04:37] PROFESSOR: Is the main problem finding suitable materials?
[04:41] JOHN: Yes. I need a professional finish, but high-quality materials are expensive.
[04:48] PROFESSOR: Projects like this raise the university's profile. Apply for a grant. I can help you complete the forms.
[04:56] JOHN: That would be great.
[04:57] PROFESSOR: I should also review your paper. In an international competition, all the technical information must be precise and comprehensive.
[05:08] JOHN: That would help a lot.
[05:10] PROFESSOR: Is there anything else?
[05:11] JOHN: Well, I'm really...
[05:15] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

content: 📌 The Spirit Bear

The bears’ feeding habits add nutrients to forest vegetation.
It now lives on a small number of [ _____ ].

Threats
Logging companies cause habitat loss through deforestation and construction of [ _____ ].
Unrestricted [ _____ ] is reducing the supply of salmon.
The bears are also threatened by a low rate of [ _____ ].

Going forward
Interested groups are cooperating.
Logging companies must improve their logging [ _____ ].
The bears’ territory needs both maintenance and [ _____ ].
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecture about the spirit bear and efforts to protect it. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Today our ecology and conservation series turns to a highly endangered member of the black bear family.

[01:00] AUDIO: Roughly one black bear in 10 is born with white fur because of an uncommon gene. Local communities call it the spirit bear. Their legends say its pale coat gives the animal unusual powers. The bear is held in such respect that residents do not tell outsiders when they have seen one, thereby protecting it from strangers.

[01:24] AUDIO: Its relationship with the old-growth rainforest is complex. The bear depends on the forest's enormous ancient trees in several ways. Their extensive roots prevent erosion along the banks of salmon streams. Protecting those banks matters because salmon are the bear's main food.

[01:46] AUDIO: The relationship also benefits the forest. When bears eat salmon, they leave skin and bones on the forest floor, adding nutrients that support rich vegetation and many other forms of life. Spirit bears now survive on only a few islands off the coast of British Columbia. Fewer than 200 may remain.

[02:10] AUDIO: Their survival therefore depends on preserving the fragile balance of the entire forest ecosystem. Habitat loss poses the greatest danger. Logging companies have removed large areas of forest and constructed roads that divide the bear's feeding grounds. Numerous hibernation sites have disappeared as well.

[02:36] AUDIO: Tree removal beside streams has harmed fishing areas, while the salmon supply is shrinking because fishing is currently unrestricted. Together, these pressures undermine the bear's survival. The danger is intensified by their consistently low rate of reproduction. What can be done, community organizations, environmental groups, and the British Columbia government are cooperating.

[03:05] AUDIO: The government now requires logging companies to improve their methods of logging. That is encouraging, but it may not be enough to secure a healthy future population. Further measures are necessary. Maintaining the spirit bear's territory is vital, but its expansion must also receive greater attention.
[03:28] AUDIO: A larger protected area would also provide space for other bears that are losing their homes. That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a woman answering questions for a local transport survey. First, you have some time to look at questions one to five. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to five.
[00:49] INTERVIEWER: Excuse me, could you spare a few minutes for a survey about transport? It won't take very long.
[00:55] LUISA: Yes, that's fine.
[00:57] INTERVIEWER: Thank you. We're conducting it for the local council. They want to learn how people travel and hear suggestions for improvements. How did you come into town today?
[01:08] LUISA: I took the bus.
[01:09] INTERVIEWER: Great. Could I have a few personal details?
[01:13] LUISA: Of course.
[01:14] INTERVIEWER: So what's your name? Louisa Hardie. Would you spell the surname, please?
[01:20] LUISA: H-A-R-D-I-E.
[01:22] INTERVIEWER: Thanks. What's your address?
[01:26] LUISA: Number 19, Whitestone Road.
[01:29] INTERVIEWER: That's in Bradfield, correct?
[01:31] LUISA: Yes.
[01:33] INTERVIEWER: Is your postcode GT7?
[01:35] LUISA: No, it's GT82LC.
[01:39] INTERVIEWER: And what do you do? Are you studying?
[01:42] LUISA: I've just completed my training, actually. I work as a hairdresser.
[01:47] INTERVIEWER: One last question in this part. Why have you come into town today?
[01:53] LUISA: I normally come to shop, but today I have an appointment with the dentist.
[01:57] INTERVIEWER: Thank you.
[02:02] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.
[02:48] INTERVIEWER: In this final section, I'd like your views on facilities and arrangements for travelling to and from work. What could the city improve?
[02:58] LUISA: When I walk home after a late shift, the streets don't feel bright enough, so better lighting would help.
[03:06] INTERVIEWER: That's a useful point.
[03:08] LUISA: It's also disappointing that the number of footpaths has been reduced. We need more of them if the council wants people to walk.
[03:16] INTERVIEWER: I see.
[03:17] LUISA: Trains should run more frequently too. I avoid them because the wait is so long.
[03:24] INTERVIEWER: Finally, what about cycling? The city is trying to persuade more residents to cycle to work.
[03:30] LUISA: Yes, I've heard about that.
[03:33] INTERVIEWER: The council and employers may both be able to make cycling more practical.
[03:38] LUISA: At my workplace, there isn't anywhere safe to park a bicycle.
[03:43] INTERVIEWER: Right.
[03:44] LUISA: I'd also have to ride uphill. On a hot day, I'd arrive feeling sweaty, so I'd need access to a shower at work.
[03:53] INTERVIEWER: Understood.
[03:55] LUISA: I'm not very confident riding on such busy roads either. If the council offered cycling training for those conditions, I'd feel much more willing to start.
[04:06] INTERVIEWER: That's extremely helpful. Thank you for your time.
[04:11] LUISA: No problem. Goodbye.
[04:17] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

passages.title: New City Development
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "New City Development"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a speaker describing two new developments in a city. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Good morning.

[00:52] AUDIO: I'm delighted to tell you about two exciting additions to the city. Brackenside Open Air Swimming Pool and the Adventure Playground in Central Park. The proposals originated with local residents during the City Council's extensive public consultation last year. Funding was then supplied by the Southwest Regional Development Commission, or SWRDC.

[01:21] AUDIO: I'll begin with Brackenside Pool. Older residents may remember the excellent open-air pool on the seafront 30 years ago. It closed after being declared unsafe. For the new heated pool, we appointed the internationally known architect Ellen Wenden.

[01:44] AUDIO: Her design combines a charming 1930s appearance, which suits neighboring buildings with modern technology. Most notably, it has a unique recycling system that treats seawater so it can be used in the pool. Local newspapers have questioned whether the facilities will be large enough for the visitor numbers we expect. The building may look smaller than it is, but capacity has been checked rigorously.

[02:17] AUDIO: The pool remains on schedule to open on June 15, and the project is within budget, thanks to the work of local contractor Hickman's. We hope many of you will attend the opening. Award-winning actress Coral White will officially open the pool, and refreshments will be served beside it. We are also organizing a public competition to choose the historical figure represented by a statue at the entrance.

[02:50] AUDIO: That identity has not yet been decided. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. I'll turn now to the Central Park Adventure playground, which received the Douglas Award for safety last week.

[03:52] AUDIO: Its global village design divides the playground into six areas, each representing a different part of the world through a characteristic feature. Asia uses rides and equipment shaped like snakes, orangutans and tigers, animals native to the region's forests. In the Antarctic area, an ice rink was too costly, so the designers created climbing blocks shaped like mountains. They considered glacier slides, but wanted to avoid an overly literal design.

[04:32] AUDIO: South America follows the El Dorado theme with games based on searching mines for precious jewels. For North America, there was considerable discussion. Cinema and jazz were considered, but the final choice was rockets and the International Space Station. Europe has the most traditional design, medieval castles and other ancient forts.

[05:04] AUDIO: Finally, Africa is represented by mosaics and trails depicting the continent's great waterways. The global playground opens on July 10th. We hope you'll come and enjoy this original new facility in the center of the city. That is the end of part two.
[05:29] AUDIO: You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

passages.title: The Life Of Thor Heyerdahl
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "The Life Of Thor Heyerdahl"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two students planning a presentation about the explorer Thor Heyerdahl. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:53] VICTOR: Shall I begin our presentation with Thor Heyerdahl's early life?
[00:58] OLIVIA: Yes. Start by describing him as a boy, especially how keen he was on collecting things.

[01:07] VICTOR: Right? He even created a small museum of his own. It's interesting that he formed his own interests instead of simply copying his parents. For instance, he refused to go hunting with his father.

[01:22] OLIVIA: He preferred learning about nature while his mother read aloud to him. He also decided quite young that he wanted to be an explorer. I think that ambition came from camping trips in Norway.
[01:37] VICTOR: Actually, climbing was the activity he devoted most of his time to as a young man.

[01:42] OLIVIA: Oh, yes. After university, he married a fellow student. They then chose to live on a small island because they wanted to experience isolation and study how severe weather affected people's way of life.

[01:59] VICTOR: Before leaving, they learned basic survival techniques such as constructing a shelter. They needed those skills for life in a remote place with very few inhabitants separated from others by the sea.
[02:15] OLIVIA: You should end your section with the radical theory Heyerdahl developed after discovering and examining mysterious ancient carvings on the island.
[02:26] VICTOR: All right.
[02:30] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.

[03:17] OLIVIA: After your section, I'll cover his adult life, beginning with his theory about Polynesian migration. Until then, academics believe that people at first reached Polynesia from Asia in the West.
[03:31] VICTOR: They considered migration from the East impossible because the nearest inhabited land was separated from the islands by an immense empty ocean.

[03:41] OLIVIA: Heyerdahl spent a long time analyzing clouds, currents, and winds to see whether such a journey could work. Scholars also argued that communities east of Polynesia had no tradition of building large ships, although Heyerdahl knew they regularly made coastal journeys in locally constructed canoes or on rafts, as his later long-distance voyage demonstrated.
[04:10] VICTOR: It was exceptionally dangerous. Sometimes I wonder whether he wanted to prove his courage by having an extraordinary adventure.
[04:19] OLIVIA: I think his main purpose was simpler. He wanted to test his theory and discover whether migration from the East was possible.
[04:29] VICTOR: Yes, that's more convincing. The war had interrupted his research for several years.
[04:36] OLIVIA: When he resumed the work and planned the voyage, was it important to complete it before anyone else?
[04:43] VICTOR: I haven't found evidence of that. His priority was building the raft with authentic ancient techniques and materials available locally.
[04:53] OLIVIA: Do we know how fast it traveled?
[04:56] VICTOR: The crossing from South America to the Pacific Island lasted 97 days.
[05:02] OLIVIA: He later visited Easter Island. We should explain why. Did he sail there in a reed boat?
[05:09] VICTOR: No, the reed boat journey happened later in Egypt.
[05:13] OLIVIA: Of course.
[05:14] VICTOR: On Easter Island, he spoke with residents about their old stone carvings and then made a statue himself to understand how the process worked.

[05:25] OLIVIA: What a remarkable life. Although many of his theories were later disproved, he influenced several fields. I think his greatest contribution was establishing the approach now called practical archaeology, recreating something from the past and the present, as he did with the raft.

[05:47] VICTOR: I'll include our sources on the final slide. I relied mainly on William Oliver's The Life and Work of Thor Heyerdahl. The research method seemed sound, but the writing style felt old-fashioned. A revised edition is needed.
[06:05] OLIVIA: I agree. The subject matter itself was difficult, though.
[06:10] VICTOR: Well, it is a complicated topic.
[06:13] OLIVIA: The book had many strengths. What did you think of?
[06:20] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecturer discussing how management may change in the future. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. I've spoken with managers from several businesses and reviewed surveys about management's future.

[00:58] AUDIO: In this seminar, I'll suggest how the field might develop over the next decade. This is not a scientific statistical study, but a set of ideas for discussion. I'll start with business markets. One major development is likely to be much greater competition as firms worldwide attempt to sell similar products.

[01:22] AUDIO: Consumers will have far more choice. Food sold in Australia, for example, may be produced in the United States, China, Finland, or many other countries. Meanwhile, mergers and takeovers are allowing large global companies to gain power that governments once held. We can all identify corporations with substantial influence, and this may sometimes benefit consumers.

[01:51] AUDIO: A third market trend concerns rapidly expanding economies such as India, China, Brazil, and Russia, where demand is rising extremely quickly. That growth is placing pressure on resources around the world. Businesses are also opening themselves to external influence. In particular, companies increasingly consult customers before making decisions.

[02:19] AUDIO: They first identify what customers want, and then supply it, rather than producing goods and attempting to sell them afterwards, as they did in the past. Environmental concerns will also oblige manufacturers to extend product life cycles and reduce pollution and waste. In some situations, this will require stronger regulation. As societies become more fluid and democratic, company structures are changing too.

[02:53] AUDIO: Businesses will place more emphasis on teams assembled to complete a particular project. Once it is finished, the team will dissolve, and new groups will form. More people now regard employment as only one element of life, rather than its centre. In countries with shrinking workforces, companies must compete to recruit staff instead of selecting from large pools of applicants.

[03:23] AUDIO: Traditional benefits such as flexible working hours can attract and retain employees. Technology also makes remote work possible from home, abroad, or almost anywhere else. Management styles will almost certainly keep evolving. Senior managers will need more than the efficiency that has always been expected of them.

[03:49] AUDIO: Above everything else, they must offer strong leadership, so their organisations can initiate and respond to change while handling competing demands and possible conflict. In much of the world, senior positions in large companies are still occupied mainly by men in their 50s and 60s. Management is likely to become more consultative and collaborative, particularly as more women take senior roles. Many shifts also reflect changes in the wider economy.

[04:24] AUDIO: Business traditionally focused on manufacturing, while the service sector remains highly important. However, we should not ignore the growing financial value of intellectual property. Books and films, for example, can generate enormous revenue through related music, games, clothing, and other products. Finally, although I have discussed companies, they must respond to a move away from spending many years with one employer.

[04:58] AUDIO: Increasing numbers of workers are becoming self-employed because this gives them freedom and control they are unlikely to obtain as employees. That concludes my remarks. Let's open the topic for discussion. That is the end of part four.
[05:21] AUDIO: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

passages.title: Early Learning Childcare Centre Enrolment Form
content: 📌 Early Learning Childcare Centre enrolment form
Parent or guardian: Carol Smith

Personal details
Child’s name: Kate
Age: [ _____ ]
Address: [ _____ ] Road, Woodside, 4032
Phone: 3345 9865

Childcare information
Days enrolled for: Monday and [ _____ ]
Start time: [ _____ ] am
Childcare group: the [ _____ ] group
Meal required each day: [ _____ ]
Medical conditions: needs [ _____ ]
Emergency contact: Jenny [ _____ ]
Phone: 3346 7523
Relationship to child: [ _____ ]

Fees
Will pay each [ _____ ]
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a mother enrolling her daughter at a childcare center. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.
[00:49] DIRECTOR: Good morning. Welcome to the Early Learning Childcare Center. How can I help?
[00:55] CAROL: Hello, I phoned last week about enrolling my daughter for next year.
[01:01] DIRECTOR: Yes, I remember. I need to take some details. You're her mother, correct?
[01:08] CAROL: That's right.
[01:10] DIRECTOR: May I have your name?
[01:12] CAROL: Carol Smith.
[01:13] DIRECTOR: And your daughter is called?
[01:15] CAROL: Kate.
[01:16] DIRECTOR: We have several groups for children aged three to five. How old is Kate?
[01:23] CAROL: She's three now, but her fourth birthday is next month.
[01:28] DIRECTOR: I'll record her age as four. Since that's how old she'll be when she begins.
[01:35] CAROL: Fine. She's very excited about both her birthday and starting here.
[01:40] DIRECTOR: What is your address?
[01:44] CAROL: 46 Wombat Road, W-O-M-B-A-T. In Woodside, postcode 4-O-3-2.
[01:54] DIRECTOR: And your telephone number?
[01:55] CAROL: It's three, three, four, five, nine, eight, six, five.
[02:00] DIRECTOR: Which days would you like Kate to attend?
[02:04] CAROL: Monday and Wednesday would suit me best.
[02:07] DIRECTOR: Monday is available, but Wednesday is already full. We could offer Thursday or Friday instead.
[02:16] CAROL: Thursday will be all right because she has swimming lessons on Friday.
[02:21] DIRECTOR: Good. We offer flexible hours. From seven thirty in the morning until six in the evening. What starting time do you need?
[02:32] CAROL: I have to reach my job in the city by nine, so I'll leave her here at eight thirty.
[02:38] DIRECTOR: That's fine. We also need to select a group. The green group is for children aged three to four, while the red group is for four to five-year-olds.
[02:51] CAROL: She's mature for her age. She can write her name and already reads a little.
[02:57] DIRECTOR: In that case, I'll place her in the red group. We can move her to green if she has any difficulties.
[03:05] CAROL: That sounds good.
[03:07] DIRECTOR: Now, meals. We can provide breakfast, lunch and dinner. She finishes early, so she won't need dinner. Will she eat breakfast at home?
[03:22] CAROL: Yes, she'll only require lunch.
[03:28] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten. Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.
[04:14] DIRECTOR: Does Kate have any medical conditions, such as asthma or hearing difficulties?
[04:21] CAROL: No, but she needs to wear glasses.
[04:23] DIRECTOR: I'll note that.
[04:25] CAROL: She's good about keeping them on because she can't see very well without them.
[04:30] DIRECTOR: I also need an emergency contact.
[04:33] CAROL: What details do you require?
[04:36] DIRECTOR: The name and number of a friend or relative we can call, if we cannot reach you.
[04:42] CAROL: Use my sister, Jenny Ball. Ball is spelled B-A-double-L. Her number is three, three, four, six, seven, five, two, three.
[04:53] DIRECTOR: So, Jenny is Kate's aunt?
[04:57] CAROL: Yes.
[04:57] DIRECTOR: Thank you. Do you have any questions?
[05:01] CAROL: How do the fees work? What is the charge each term?
[05:05] DIRECTOR: For two days and the hours you selected, the total is four hundred fifty dollars.
[05:13] CAROL: Must I pay now?
[05:14] DIRECTOR: No. We send in voices after the children begin. You may pay at the end of each term or receive a small discount by paying every month.
[05:27] CAROL: I'll pay monthly. That's easier for budgeting and I don't know the term dates yet.
[05:33] DIRECTOR: That is simpler for us too. That completes the form. Would you like me to show you around?
[05:45] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

passages.title: Dolphin Reservation Trust
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Dolphin Reservation Trust"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear an interview with the representative of the Dolphin Conservation Trust. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15. Today, we welcome Alice Bussell from the Dolphin Conservation Trust.

[00:56] AUDIO: Alice, could you describe the organization? Its purpose is to protect dolphins in seas around the world. We raise awareness of the pollution and other threats these animals face. The Trust began 10 years ago and is among the country's fastest growing animal charities, although it remains small beside the largest conservation groups.

[01:21] AUDIO: We're particularly proud of our educational work. Last year, we visited many schools and spoke to young people aged 5 to 18. Children make up about 35% of our membership. We use donations to support campaigns, including efforts to change fishing policies.

[01:43] AUDIO: We hope to employ our first full-time dolphin biologist soon to monitor populations. At present, many people volunteer their time in observation work, administration and several other roles. Last year, the Charity Commission gave us an award for education. It didn't provide much additional money, but it made our work far more widely known and understood.

[02:11] AUDIO: We hope this publicity may eventually increase membership. Can people see dolphins in British waters? Yes, in several places. We run a major project in eastern Scotland, an area that has long sheltered dolphins because there is little shipping.

[02:31] AUDIO: Oil companies now want to expand exploration there. We oppose the plan because the exploration produces intense underwater noise, even though serious oil pollution is unlikely. That noise prevents dolphins from resting and socialising. That issue first sparked my interest in dolphin conservation.

[02:55] AUDIO: I had never seen a dolphin and hadn't been especially interested at school. Then I found a book about dolphins forced from their Moray Firth home by oil companies and about a child who campaigned to protect them. I couldn't stop reading it. Before you hear the rest of the interview, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

[03:54] AUDIO: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20. Listeners will want to know how they can help. Could you explain the adopt a dolphin scheme? Sponsors choose a dolphin and receive its photograph and regular news.

[04:14] AUDIO: Four dolphins currently feature in the scheme. Moondancer, Echo, Kiwi and Samson. Echo has been difficult to find and our observers haven't seen him at all this year, though we hope he'll appear soon. The other three have been very visible.

[04:35] AUDIO: Samson and Moondancer are often photographed together, but Kiwi approaches cameras so frequently that she has been photographed hundreds of times. More than any of the others, each has a distinct personality. Moondancer moves through the water with elegant curves, while Samson is remarkably energetic and constantly leaps above the surface. Kiwi is actually the youngest dolphin, but Samson is the most recent addition to the adoption scheme.

[05:11] AUDIO: Kiwi is noisy so we can identify her quickly. Echo and Moondancer also make plenty of sound. Moondancer, however, is particularly easy to recognise because her back fin is unusually large. They certainly sound fascinating.
[05:30] AUDIO: That is the end of part two. You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two theatre students discussing a recent production and a study abroad option. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

[01:20] MIA: What gave you the initial idea?
[01:23] ROB: My grandfather was a doctor before he retired, so I based the character on him.
[01:28] MIA: Did you ask him about his work?
[01:32] ROB: He probably has many stories, but he rarely discusses his job. Still, he has a natural authority.
[01:40] MIA: How did you reproduce that quality?
[01:43] ROB: I imagined how he would have behaved years ago, sitting in his consulting room and listening to patients.
[01:50] MIA: Good. Explain that process in the report.
[01:54] ROB: Right.

[01:56] MIA: You should also discuss atmosphere. In the opening waiting room scene, we had to convey how monotonous village life was in the 1950s. There was a long silence before anyone spoke, and then the characters repeatedly used the same comments, such as asking whether it was cold.
[02:17] ROB: Everyone also wore gray or brown and sat in one row.
[02:22] MIA: Include all those production choices.
[02:25] ROB: I also need to analyze my role in the group and what I discovered about myself. I sometimes became frustrated when we couldn't agree.
[02:35] MIA: Did anybody take charge?
[02:39] ROB: Sophia did. I didn't mind, because she gave us precise instructions about what the production required. Having clear guidance made me feel more comfortable.
[02:49] MIA: Sophia also carried out some helpful research.
[02:54] ROB: Yes. She found 1950s articles describing shifts in relationships between parents and children and between the public and authority figures, such as police officers and bank managers.
[03:09] MIA: Did the group encounter practical difficulties?
[03:13] ROB: During the final rehearsal, everything worked until the last scene, when the doctor's first patient appears alone.
[03:20] MIA: The patient in the wheelchair?
[03:22] ROB: Yes. He delivers a long speech in darkness under a single spotlight. The light jammed and pointed at the wrong side of the stage, but we managed to repair it.
[03:35] MIA: And it worked properly during the performance.
[03:41] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
[04:28] ROB: While you're here, would you recommend the year abroad option?
[04:32] MIA: Definitely. It's an excellent opportunity to spend a year studying in another country.
[04:39] ROB: I'd like to apply, but places seem very competitive.

[04:42] MIA: They are limited. During your second year, you must work hard across every theater studies module. Only students with high marks receive places, so you need to demonstrate strong ability in the subject.
[04:58] ROB: How did you decide where to study?

[05:00] MIA: I wanted a program connected to my plans after graduation. I therefore chose an institution emphasizing acting rather than directing. You must check that its academic focus is relevant to your aims. About six months before departure, you email your three preferred choices to the scheme coordinator.
[05:22] MIA: A friend missed the deadline and lost her first choice, so make certain you submit everything on time.
[05:30] ROB: Don't applicants also write a personal statement?
[05:33] MIA: Yes.
[05:35] ROB: I'll ask final year students for help and see whether they'll share their statements.

[05:40] MIA: That's sensible, and I can show you mine. While you're abroad, avoid my mistake. I became so absorbed in the experience that I failed to organize my return for the final year. Stay in contact and plan your final year optional modules, or you may miss the specialisms you want.
[06:01] ROB: Understood.
[06:05] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

passages.title: Self-Regulatory Focus Theory' And Leadership
content: 📌 Self-regulatory focus theory and leadership

Self-regulatory focus theory
People focus on approaching pleasure or avoiding pain.
Promotion goals centre on [ _____ ].
Prevention goals emphasise avoiding punishment.
Factors affecting people’s focus

The chronic factor
Originates in a person’s [ _____ ]

The [ _____ ] factor
Promotion goals are more likely when a person is with a [ _____ ]
Prevention goals are more likely when dealing with a boss

How people’s focus affects them
Promotion focus: people consider an ideal version of themselves, their [ _____ ] and their gains.
Prevention focus: people consider their “ought” self and their obligations.

Leaders
Leadership behaviour and [ _____ ] affect people’s focus.

Transformational leaders
Give particular attention to followers’ [ _____ ]
Communicate a clear [ _____ ] with passion
Inspire promotion focus in followers

Transactional leaders
Establish [ _____ ] that make expectations clear
Emphasise the consequences of mistakes
Inspire prevention focus in followers

Conclusion
Promotion focus is suitable for work requiring [ _____ ].
Prevention focus suits work such as surgery.
Leaders’ actions affect which focus people use.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecture about self-regulatory focus theory and leadership. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Today I'll discuss self-regulatory focus theory and how leaders' actions can influence the way followers respond to situations.

[01:01] AUDIO: The theory developed by Torrey Higgins proposes that at any moment people are motivated either to move towards pleasure or to avoid pain. These basic motives produce different kinds of goals. Promotion goals emphasize achievement while prevention goals center on avoiding punishment. In any particular situation, our thoughts may lean towards promotion or prevention.

[01:29] AUDIO: Two factors determine the stronger focus. The first is chronic and derives from personality. Each individual has an underlying tendency towards one type of goal. The second is situational, meaning that our surroundings can shift us towards either set of goals.

[01:50] AUDIO: For example, time spent with a friend makes us more likely to anticipate pleasure and pursue promotion goals. By contrast, while completing an important assignment for a boss, we usually concentrate on preventing mistakes and adopt prevention goals. Research shows that our current focus changes how we think. Under a promotion focus, people picture their ideal selves and consider their aspirations and potential gains.

[02:21] AUDIO: Because they pay less attention to possible losses, their thinking becomes more positive and they feel inspired to change. Under a prevention focus, people consider the person they ought to be and what others expect from them. Their attention turns to obligations. This can increase anxiety and encourage them to avoid situations involving possible loss.

[02:49] AUDIO: Having explained the two focuses, I'll consider how leadership behavior, or leadership style, can shape the focus. Followers adopt in a given situation. Leadership discussions often distinguish transformational from transactional leaders. Transformational leaders concentrate on the development of their followers.

[03:14] AUDIO: Their words and actions emphasize change and they passionately express a clear vision. This encourages followers to imagine future possibilities and adopt a promotion focus. Transactional leaders, in contrast, establish clear structures that specify exactly what followers must do. Although they explain the rewards for following instructions, they place greater emphasis on punishment or the loss of rewards when behavior does not improve.

[03:50] AUDIO: By stressing the consequences of errors, they inspire a prevention focus. Neither focus is inherently superior. A designer working in a field that demands innovation will probably benefit from promotion focus. Prevention focus encourages caution and high quality work, making it suitable for occupations such as surgery.

[04:17] AUDIO: The central finding is that leaders' actions can strongly influence which focus people bring to a situation. That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

content: 📌 Thorndyke's Builders

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a customer speaking to a builder about work needed in her flat and garden. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now, listen carefully and answer questions one to six.
[00:52] MR THORNDYKE: Thorndykes builders.
[00:54] EDITH: Good morning. Am I speaking to Mr Thorndyke?
[00:58] MR THORNDYKE: Yes, how can I help?
[00:59] EDITH: Several things in my flat need painting or repairing. I wondered whether you could do the work.
[01:06] MR THORNDYKE: I'm sure I can help. First, I'll take some details. How did you hear about us?
[01:13] EDITH: My friend May Hampton recommended you. You worked for her a couple of years ago.
[01:18] MR THORNDYKE: I remember. She lived at West Park Flats. What is your name?
[01:24] EDITH: Edith Pargetter.
[01:25] MR THORNDYKE: Could you spell the surname?
[01:26] EDITH: P-A-R-G-E-double T-E-R.
[01:34] MR THORNDYKE: Do you also live at West Park Flats?
[01:37] EDITH: No. East Park Flats. Number four.
[01:40] MR THORNDYKE: That's across the road and rather difficult to reach, isn't it?
[01:45] EDITH: Yes. The building is behind the library.
[01:49] MR THORNDYKE: What telephone number should I use? Eight, seven, five, nine, three, four.
[01:57] EDITH: But I'm usually out during afternoons and evenings.
[02:01] MR THORNDYKE: So mornings are the best time to call?
[02:04] EDITH: Yes.
[02:06] MR THORNDYKE: I'll be driving a van. Where can I park?
[02:10] EDITH: On the opposite side of the road from the entrance beside the post box.
[02:14] MR THORNDYKE: Thank you.
[02:15] EDITH: Could you provide a fully itemized quotation?
[02:19] MR THORNDYKE: Certainly. I'll list every job separately and show all the prices.
[02:24] EDITH: That would be helpful.
[02:31] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten. Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.
[03:17] MR THORNDYKE: What work is required?
[03:19] EDITH: The most urgent job is in the kitchen. Weather damage has cracked the glass in the door and it needs fixing.
[03:27] MR THORNDYKE: You mean the glass must be replaced?
[03:30] EDITH: Yes. As soon as possible.
[03:33] MR THORNDYKE: I can come tomorrow morning and deal with that immediately.
[03:36] EDITH: Thank you. The remaining work is less urgent.
[03:40] MR THORNDYKE: I'll note everything.
[03:42] EDITH: I'd like part of the kitchen painted.
[03:45] MR THORNDYKE: All the walls?
[03:46] EDITH: No, only the wall above the cooker. It has become greasy.
[03:50] MR THORNDYKE: For a proper finish, I'll strip away the old paint and apply plaster about one week before painting.
[03:59] EDITH: That's fine. May also said you do garden work.
[04:03] MR THORNDYKE: I do.
[04:04] EDITH: One fence at the far end of the garden needs replacing.
[04:08] MR THORNDYKE: That should be straightforward. I'll visit tomorrow morning to inspect everything.
[04:14] EDITH: Excellent. Thank you.
[04:15] MR THORNDYKE: I'll see you tomorrow at...
[04:20] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

passages.title: Manham Port
content:
Tourist attractionDetailsCopper mineSpecially adapted miners’ [ _____ ] take visitors into the mountain. 
The mine is [ _____ ] and closed in, making it unsuitable for children and animals.Village schoolClassrooms and a special exhibition of [ _____ ]. 
Taking a [ _____ ] is advisable.The George, an old sailing shipThe ship’s wheel has been recovered and restored. 
Children should not use the [ _____ ].
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a guide describing the history and attractions of Manham Port. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15. Welcome to Manham Port, where a thousand years of history have been recreated.

[00:58] AUDIO: Families can explore the copper mine and machinery models, dress in 19th century costume for photographs, and discover how people once lived, worked, studied and played. Manham lies in peaceful countryside on a bend of the River Avon. The port developed here because this is the highest point that boats can navigate. Cargo could conveniently be transferred between river vessels and the sea more than 23 miles away.

[01:33] AUDIO: A small port existed when tin was found nearby around 900 years ago. Its dramatic expansion came later during the Industrial Revolution when demand for all kinds of metal rose sharply. By the late 19th century, lead, copper, manganese and arsenic were also shipped from Manham. Originally, ores were processed close to the mines.

[02:03] AUDIO: As demand increased, however, smelting required enormous furnaces and the area lacked sufficient coal. Mineral-bearing rock, therefore, had to be transported elsewhere for processing. During the 20th century, the port declined and thousands of workers left the area. Buildings deteriorated and Manham was almost forgotten.

[02:30] AUDIO: The Manham Trust was then established to preserve its historical resources. Volunteers cleared vegetation to reveal the original installations. Paid specialists compared these remains with historic maps and began rebuilding the complete port complex. The aim is to restore Manham to its peak as the country's greatest copper port.
[03:00] AUDIO: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20. What can visitors see today? Begin at the Copper Mine.

[03:53] AUDIO: Adapted miners' trains carry passengers deep into the mountain, along seams, once worked by hundreds of people. Notice the large pumps that removed water. The mine is dark and enclosed, so children under five and dogs must not enter. Next, visit the village school.

[04:14] AUDIO: Explore the classrooms and the exceptional exhibition of games, one of the largest collections anywhere. We recommend joining a guided tour, which allows you to ask questions. Near the school stands an old sailing vessel called the George. Visitors may board and inspect its cabins.

[04:36] AUDIO: Its wheel was missing until a fisherman recovered it from the silt five years ago. It has been restored to its original position. Take care on the ladders leading to the lower deck and do not allow young children to use them. We hope you enjoy Manham Port and recommend it to your friends.
[05:01] AUDIO: That is the end of part two. You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

questions.prompt: Why was a port first established at Manham?
options: It was protected from enemy attack.
It was convenient for river transport.
It occupied a favourable coastal position.

passages.title: Placement In The Workplace
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Placement In The Workplace"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two students discussing a work placement. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:50] TIM: Hi, Laura. Could you tell me about the placement you completed last summer? I'm considering one myself.
[00:58] LAURA: Of course.
[00:59] TIM: Was yours with an environmental services company?

[01:03] LAURA: Yes, it's a small firm that needed a company brochure. I wanted business experience because I'm interested in occupational psychology and commercial settings. I was responsible for the entire project.
[01:18] TIM: Which skills did you develop? Did you create the artwork and layout?
[01:23] LAURA: We employed a professional photographer. I used some I.T. skills to combine text from marketing leaflets. But I had done that before.
[01:34] TIM: Did you improve at organizing your time and deciding priorities? You used to find that difficult.

[01:40] LAURA: Definitely. Meeting the deadline created considerable pressure. I also improved my communication, explaining ideas and stating my views because I met the marketing manager weekly and reported my progress.
[01:58] TIM: So the placement benefited you.
[02:00] LAURA: Very much. And the company gained two.
[02:04] TIM: Using a professional advertising agency would have cost considerably more, wouldn't it?

[02:10] LAURA: Yes, about 250 percent more. Although we produced everything internally, the final brochure looked professional and improved the company's image immediately. I used its powerful computer and borrowed scanning software from the university.
[02:28] TIM: In time, it may attract clients and raise sales.
[02:33] LAURA: That is the intention.
[02:39] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.
[03:25] TIM: I think I'll apply for a placement. What should I do first?
[03:30] LAURA: A government agency called Step organizes placements. Begin by obtaining its information booklet, which may be available online.
[03:39] TIM: The psychology department keeps printed copies. I'll collect one there.
[03:45] LAURA: After reading it, discuss the possibilities with somebody.
[03:49] TIM: Perhaps my personal tutor.
[03:51] LAURA: A university careers officer would know more about the employment market.
[03:57] TIM: All right.
[03:58] LAURA: Once you decide, register with Step using the address in the booklet. You'll be assigned a mentor to supervise the application.
[04:08] TIM: Then do I simply wait for news?
[04:11] LAURA: Be proactive. Check the Internet for new placement alerts and updates. Mentors should inform you, but don't depend entirely on them.
[04:22] TIM: Should I contact companies directly?
[04:25] LAURA: Generally, no. If a company wants to interview you, its personnel department sends the invitation by letter or email.
[04:33] TIM: Do I reply to that department?
[04:36] LAURA: Yes. Step becomes involved again only after a job offer.
[04:43] TIM: After the interview, I should tell my mentor the result, including whether I receive and accept an offer.
[04:50] LAURA: Correct. The mentor informs the careers office once the placement is confirmed.
[04:56] TIM: Is that everything?
[05:00] LAURA: After accepting, you may need a reference because the offer is conditional. Ask your personal tutor who knows your academic ability and qualities such as reliability.
[05:13] TIM: Thanks. I'm beginning to look forward.
[05:20] NARRATOR: That is the end of part three. You now have one minute to check your answers to part three.

passages.title: Nanotechnology
content: 📌 Uses of Nanotechnology

Transport
Nanotechnology could enable stronger [ _____ ] to be developed.
Aircraft would be far lighter.
[ _____ ] travel would become available to the public.

Technology
Computers would become smaller and faster and possess greater [ _____ ].
[ _____ ] energy would cost less.

The environment
Nanorobots could reconstruct the ozone layer.
Pollutants such as [ _____ ] could be filtered out of water.
Manufacturing would generate no [ _____ ].

Health and medicine
New food-production methods could eliminate famine.
Medical [ _____ ] could be assessed more quickly.
Life expectancy might increase.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecture about nanotechnology and its possible applications. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Today we'll examine nanotechnology, an important scientific field.

[00:57] AUDIO: Nano means extremely small, so this is science and engineering at the level of atoms and molecules. By controlling and rearranging atoms, it may eventually be possible to manufacture almost anything. Science at this scale therefore has very large implications. Nanotechnology promises enormous benefits, but every emerging technology has early difficulties.

[01:28] AUDIO: In this case, the public frequently misunderstands what the technology can actually do. Science fiction stories have encouraged fears of invisible robots monitoring people or reproducing until they dominate the world. How should such a powerful field be managed? Some scientists argue that nanoparticles should be treated as new chemicals with independent safety testing and clear labels.

[01:58] AUDIO: They also recommend greater caution when these particles are handled in laboratories and factories. Other people call for new products such as cosmetics to be withdrawn and for parts of nanotechnology research to stop temporarily. My own view is that exploration and practical development should continue. Most scientists would support safeguards against unethical applications, but we cannot assume every innovation is harmful.

[02:30] AUDIO: As with any technology, the crucial issue is how it is used. In transport, nanotechnology may produce stronger, more durable metals that are nearly unbreakable, lighter and more flexible. Aircraft could weigh 50 times less than current models. These improvements would also reduce the cost of space travel, making it accessible to ordinary people.

[02:59] AUDIO: Computer components could be reduced to minute dimensions. Future computers may operate faster, provide a million times more memory and still be no larger than a sugar cube. Power generation could also change. Nanotechnology should lower the cost of solar cells, making solar energy far more affordable.

[03:23] AUDIO: Environmental applications may be even broader. Tiny airborne robots could help rebuild the ozone layer. On a local scale, the technology could remove oil and other pollutants from water after environmental disasters. If products are constructed atom by atom, manufacturers would use only the exact materials needed, producing no waste.

[03:49] AUDIO: The ability to reproduce almost anything also has major consequences for health. Food-producing machines might one day eradicate famine. Medicine may experience the greatest impact. Tiny biosensors could analyze medical tests in minutes rather than days.

[04:09] AUDIO: Some researchers even speculate that nanorobots might slow aging and extend human life. These possibilities are exciting, although nobody can say precisely when they will become available. That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
